summary:
Virginia stands under the United States federal framework, and the exposures a trans visitor is most likely to meet are set at national level: identity documents, airport screening, visa decisions, federal custody and access to care. State-level conditions in Virginia are addressed separately below.

Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020).

The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth. New passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Screening at US checkpoints carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. Several governments have responded. In April 2025 CNN reported advisories issued by several countries about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

Facility restrictions vary sharply by state. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

State document rules are tightening. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

Visa screening carries its own exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement refusing visas to trans athletes entering the United States to compete in women's sporting events; applicants are flagged with the internal marking "SWS25", and listing a gender other than one's assigned sex is treated as grounds for a permanent ban on fraud grounds.

Federal custody presents documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported denial of care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Care access is constrained. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Virginia itself sits in the Low-Risk States group of the July 2026 national legal risk assessment, alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia. The same assessment names Virginia with Arizona as a state that enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies which, because of state-specific factors, appear unlikely to extend to adults.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 national legal risk assessment groups nine jurisdictions as low risk for trans people, and its placement of Virginia there is a comparative finding rather than a statement that Virginia law is protective. The assessment draws the same distinction for Virginia and Arizona: youth-targeted measures exist in both, and in both the assessment expects them to stop at the age of majority.

National direction of travel runs against the Virginia rating. The same assessment reports four states flagged "Do Not Travel" as of July 2026, with Idaho the most recent addition, and describes the 2026 legislative season as continuing to degrade trans rights while federal measures drove nationwide trends. Kansas is described by rights groups as a template other legislatures may copy.

Foreign government advisories about travelling to the United States are a documented response to federal document and data rules, with Axios recording at least eight European countries adjusting entry guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens in March 2025 and CNN reporting further advisories in April 2025.

Court intervention is the main counterweight to the federal measures. Several of the executive and agency actions on care, documents and facilities have been blocked or enjoined, and litigation is live: the ACLU's suit against the State Department covers seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal publishes guidance on documentation and federal records.
localsOnly:
Virginia has enacted anti-trans policies directed at young people, and the July 2026 national legal risk assessment treats them as confined to minors on state-specific grounds, expecting them not to extend to adults resident in the state.

Residents held in federal custody fall under Federal Bureau of Prisons policies adopted from 2026 that mandate conversion-therapy approaches for transgender inmates, including short haircuts, withdrawal of hormone medication and substitution of psychiatric treatment, with the Bureau no longer reporting transgender prisoner numbers from 2025. Transgender people in ICE custody have reported forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and sexual abuse when they refuse.

Residents under 18 face the proposed October 2025 rule barring Medicaid reimbursement for transgender patients, the July 2025 removal of specialised LGBTQ youth services from the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and a subpoena campaign in summer 2025 in which the Department of Justice sought full records of patients under 19 from more than 20 hospitals.

Facility rules for residents are a patchwork across the country: bans apply in nine states and one territory in K-12 schools and some government buildings, 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states criminalise trans bathroom use in certain circumstances. Which of those categories applies inside Virginia is not settled by the sources below.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the specific statutory content of Virginia's youth-targeting measures is not set out in the available inventory, so their exact scope and enforcement cannot be described here.

Unresolved: the Movement Advancement Project equality map cited for the state-by-state list of facility bans now returns HTTP 404 at the address used, the page having moved. The ban counts reproduced above come from the risk assessment's citation of that map rather than from direct inspection, and whether Virginia falls among the 29 states with no facility ban, or among those with restrictions, is not stated.

Not sourced: whether Virginia maintains its own birth-certificate or driver's-licence marker rules for transgender residents. Kansas is documented as of February 2026; no equivalent Virginia provision appears in the inventory.

Not sourced: Virginia-level data on hate-crime prosecution, partner recognition or police complaints involving transgender visitors or residents. The findings above on violence, custody abuse and document confiscation are national in origin and are not tied to Virginia by the inventory.
